20250228_7476506728750697750.t: A North Cardinal Mark indicates safe water to the north, identified by two upward-pointing black cones, yellow and black stripes, and a continuous quick-flashing white light at night.

20250228_7476507101481749782.t: An East cardinal mark indicates safe water to the East through base-to-base black cones, black and yellow horizontal bands, and a white light flashing in groups of three.

20250228_7476508123457686806.t: A South Cardinal Mark features downward-pointing cones, yellow and black stripes, and a light characteristic of six quick flashes plus one long flash to indicate safe water to the south.

20250228_7476508810593668375.t: A West Cardinal mark features cones pointing towards each other, black and yellow stripes, and a light pattern of quick flashing white light in groups of nine, indicating safe water lies to the west.

20250315_7482035578490473750.t: Special marks are solid yellow buoys used to indicate non-hazard features like cables or pipelines, displaying a yellow light with a unique rhythm at night.

20250315_7482035691975626006.t: An isolated danger mark sits directly over a hazard, identified by horizontal black and red bands, two black sphere topmarks, and a group flashing white light (Fl(2)) at night.

20250315_7482035931592019222.t: Safe water marks have red and white vertical stripes, a red spherical topmark, and display white light patterns such as a long flash at night to indicate navigable deep water.

20250315_7482035982267813122.t: Learn how to identify a new danger mark by its vertical blue and yellow stripes in the day and alternating blue and yellow light at night.

20250318_7483146603738483990.t: Explains the anchor light requirements for vessels under and over 50 meters length under COLREGs.

20250318_7483149317268638978.t: Explains the navigation light configuration and visibility ranges for power-driven vessels over 50 meters underway at night, and how to identify their aspect.

20250319_7483479165237218582.t: A vessel that is Not Under Command (NUC) and making way through the water at night must display two all-round red lights vertically along with its sidelights and stern light.

20250319_7483523128749051158.t: Vessels restricted in their ability to manoeuvre display a vertical red-white-red light pattern and must be given way by other vessels.

20250321_7484330446248103190.t: Vessels actively trawling at night must display green-over-white lights along with standard navigation lights when making way.

20250325_7485719213840010518.t: Vessels engaged in dredging or underwater operations display red-white-red lights for restricted manoeuvrability, green lights for clear passage, red lights for obstructed side, and standard navigation lights when making headway.

20250330_7487603693819333910.t: Under COLREG Rule 14, when two power-driven vessels meet head-on, both must alter course to starboard to pass port-to-port.

20250404_7489426660144549142.t: This video explains the purpose of a MAYDAY distress call on VHF Channel 16 and provides a complete example script detailing vessel identity, position, nature of distress, and assistance required.

20250407_7490613866091580694.t: Learn when to issue a PAN PAN urgency signal on VHF Channel 16 and how to structure the distress broadcast.

20250411_7492030103619177750.t: Learn how Search and Rescue Transponders (SART) function by emitting distinctive dot patterns on nearby marine radar screens to assist rescuers.

20250415_7493511535214595350.t: Sécurité is the international VHF safety call used by coast guards and mariners to broadcast navigational and meteorological warnings.

20250508_7501965970961976598.t: Under COLREGs Rule 15 for crossing situations, the vessel with the other on its starboard side must give way early and substantially, typically by altering course to starboard.

20250613_7515420855942384918.t: Rule 13 of COLREGs dictates that any vessel overtaking another must keep clear, defined as approaching from more than 22.5 degrees abaft the beam or seeing only a sternlight at night.

20260228_7612065465409555734.t: A north cardinal mark indicates safe water to its north, identified by two upward-pointing black cones and a continuous quick-flashing white light at night.

20260302_7612786849177816342.t: An East Cardinal Mark is identified by two black cones placed base-to-base and displays a quick flashing white light in groups of three at night to signal safe water to the east.

20260304_7613316707804876054.t: Special marks are solid yellow buoys used to indicate specific features such as cable areas or recreation zones rather than hazards.

20260315_7617511432627801347.t: An isolated danger mark is positioned directly over a hazard and can be identified by its black and red horizontal bands, two black sphere topmarks, and a white light flashing twice at night.

20260315_7617511480132472087.t: Special marks are solid yellow marks used to indicate special areas or features rather than hazards, displaying a yellow light at night.

20260315_7617511612349500694.t: Learn how to identify a safe water mark by its vertical red and white stripes, red spherical topmark, and light characteristics.

20260315_7617511644767325462.t: Special marks are yellow buoyage features used to designate specific areas like pipelines or cables rather than navigational hazards.

20260318_7618519783184551190.t: Learners will understand the navigation light requirements for a power-driven vessel over 50 meters and how to identify its aspect at night.

20260318_7618520537022598402.t: Vessels at anchor must display all-round white lights according to COLREGs Rule 30, with requirements differing based on whether the vessel is under 50 meters, over 50 meters, or over 100 meters.

20260319_7618867528261012758.t: Explains the navigation light configuration and obligations for a vessel Not Under Command (NUC) making way at night.

20260330_7623056446078471446.t: Under IRPCS Rule 14, two power-driven vessels meeting on reciprocal courses must both alter course to starboard to pass port to port.

20260404_7624782093339397398.t: This video explains the purpose of a Mayday distress call on VHF Channel 16 and demonstrates the correct format for transmitting one.

20260407_7626007804033240342.t: Learn the definition and proper broadcast structure of a Pan-Pan urgency signal on VHF channel 16.

20260411_7627419157998374166.t: This clip explains how a search and rescue transponder (SART) works by displaying a distinctive blip pattern on nearby radar screens to pinpoint a distressed vessel's location.

20260415_7628851795602722070.t: Learners will understand how Securité calls are structured and used to transmit important safety and navigational hazard broadcasts over VHF radio.

20260613_7650815215277198614.t: Rule 13 of the COLREGs mandates that any vessel overtaking another from more than 22.5 degrees abaft the beam—indicated at night by seeing only its sternlight—must keep clear, overriding all other collision avoidance rules.

20260702_7658033754648284438.t: When a stand-on vessel encounters a crossing situation from the port bow, it must maintain course and speed while monitoring the give-way vessel, taking early action to avoid crossing ahead if the give-way vessel fails to keep clear.

20260714_7662148471243148566.t: Learn how to read metric draft marks on a hull, calculate mean draft and trim, differentiate draft from air draft, and ensure adequate under-keel clearance while accounting for squat and tide.

20260715_7662149199210745110.t: In IALA Region A, vessels returning from seaward keep red port hand marks to port and green starboard hand marks to starboard.

20260715_7662710914327514390.t: In restricted visibility, COLREGs Rule 19 applies, removing stand-on/give-way obligations so both vessels must reduce speed and take avoiding action based on radar and sound signals.

20260716_7662150830971358487.t: Learn how vessel speed, depth-to-draft ratio, hull shape, and channel confinement cause squat, reducing underkeel clearance, and how to estimate it using the Barrass formula.

20260716_7663095862305885462.t: Rule 18 establishes the hierarchy of give-way responsibilities between vessels based on their manoeuvrability.

20260716_7663247528988642582.t: A concise guide explaining the essential terminology for every part of a sailboat, including the hull, spars, rigging, and sails.

20260717_7662150223283653910.t: Air draft is the height from the waterline to the vessel's highest fixed point, which varies with cargo, trim, and tide, determining safe clearance under bridges and power cables.

20260719_7662152650045082902.t: Learn how the Plimsoll mark and load line markings indicate maximum draft and freeboard across different water densities and seasonal zones.

20260719_7664284540734622998.t: Understand how marine radar measures target range and bearing through radio echoes, and learn its operational limits under COLREGs Rule 7.

20260720_7662153729885408534.t: Understand the crucial distinctions between heel, list, and angle of loll, including why angle of loll is caused by a negative initial metacentric height (GM) and how to safely correct it without capsizing.

20260721_7662158343246499094.t: Learners will understand how metacentric height (GM) determines ship stability, distinguishing between stiff and tender movement, angle of loll, and the impacts of free surface effect.

20260722_7662158767018085654.t: Learn how to recognize COLREGs day shapes for various vessel statuses including not under command, at anchor, aground, RAM, constrained by draught, motoring sailing vessels, fishing, and towing.

20260723_7662159902420389142.t: Learners will understand the definitions, etymologies, memory tricks, and night sidelight color conventions for port and starboard.

20260724_7662161761583353110.t: Learners will understand how to use the TVMDC rule to convert between true, magnetic, and compass courses by applying variation and deviation.

20260725_7662162420458212630.t: Learners will understand the main points of sail relative to wind direction, from the no-go zone up to a run, as well as basic port and starboard tack give-way rules.

20260726_7664263375391706390.t: Covers the essential sequence of actions required during a man-overboard emergency, from alarm and Mayday transmission to final approach into the wind.
